description: We are Team KAIROS, a team passionate about technology, electronics, and innovation. We love learning, creating new things, and working together to achieve great ideas.
summary: HIFIC (Historical Fire Calendar) is a web page where, by selecting an area, we convert MODIS hotspots into their VIIRS equivalent in order to join 2000–2011 (MODIS only) with 2012 onward (VIIRS) into a single fire activity calendar. Without that conversion, 12 years of history cannot be compared with the current record, which would leave that data obsolete. The project gives emergency managers, scientists, and environmental researchers a tool to compare whether current hotspot records are normal against the historical record.
details:
HIFIC

HIFIC is a web application that shows, in a monthly calendar, how many fire hotspots were detected worldwide from the year 2000 to today. The record is split between two NASA sensors that cannot be directly compared: MODIS (since 2000, 1 km pixel) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m pixel and much more sensitive).

To join them, we developed a formula that converts each MODIS fire point into its equivalent in VIIRS points. It starts from a base weight and adjusts it according to fire intensity (FRP), the number of fires in that month, and the dry season. We calculated the coefficients with a Poisson regression using 2012–2025, the years in which both sensors operated at the same time.

That way, 2000–2011 ends up on the same scale as VIIRS, and from 2012 onward the calendar uses the real VIIRS data. The page processes FIRMS CSV files automatically: it cleans them, applies the formula, sums by month, and displays the result. It also connects to the FIRMS API to include the most recent data in near real time.

It lets you see 25 years of fire activity on a single, coherent scale, without the artificial jump that would appear in 2012 if the data were combined without conversion. An emergency or land manager can see at a glance which months concentrate the most fires, recognize whether the current month is unusual compared to the historical record, and plan surveillance and resources before the critical season.

Each month indicates which source it comes from (real VIIRS or equivalent) and with what level of confidence, so the user knows how much they can rely on each data point.

We hope HIFIC helps first responders, early warning services, scientists, and land managers anticipate critical periods instead of reacting once the fire is already active. It also rescues more than a decade of history (2000–2011) that today cannot be compared with current data, and prepares the record for when MODIS stops operating and VIIRS becomes the only source.

We are starting with the Dominican Republic, but the method can be applied to any region by recalculating the coefficients with its own data.

Instead of multiplying everything by a fixed factor or using only the pixel size difference, which was the first thing we tried, each fire point receives its own weight according to how the fire behaves. An intense fire is worth more because VIIRS sees it spread across several pixels. In a quiet month each point is worth a bit more, because small fires, which MODIS cannot detect, weigh more there.

In addition, we validated the method honestly: we converted each year from 2012–2025 without using it in the calibration and compared it with the real VIIRS, as if it were a historical year.

We took into account:

• Data quality: only vegetation fires, confidence-level filters, a single VIIRS satellite as reference, and no preliminary data in the historical years.

• Physical differences between sensors: different overpass times, clouds and haze, and the resolution difference. That is why each month shows a probable range in addition to its value.

• Available satellites: between 2000 and mid-2002 only Terra existed, so those months use different coefficients.

• Ease of use: a calendar is understood without technical knowledge, and months without data appear in gray so they are not confused with months without fire.

• Security and continuity: the API key stays on the server and the website can keep receiving new data.

In the future, we aim for this website to have real-time data from NASA’s database, so that access to this resource expands to all countries in the world, integrating a mobile app that lets people receive notifications about the presence of hotspots near them. As the final scope of the prototype, we would like to adapt an AI model trained to analyze historical data and make predictions that serve as a tool for different organizations and open the door to prevention and to saving lives and ecosystems.
